analysis.one_liner: Creates federal grants for free, full-day preschool for four-year-olds from low- and moderate-income families.
analysis.headline: The Senate education committee reported the bill the day it was introduced, but it drew no cosponsors and never came to a Senate floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would send federal matching grants to states to pay for free, full-day prekindergarten for three- and four-year-olds from families earning up to 200% of the poverty line, with states pitching in a growing share over time. Programs would have to meet quality rules: classes of no more than 20, one adult per 10 children, teachers with bachelor's degrees paid on par with K-12 teachers, and built-in health, nutrition, and family support services. It would also fund Early Head Start partnerships with child care providers and a Senate statement of support for home-visiting programs for at-risk families. The bill never received a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Three- and four-year-olds from families at or below 200% of the poverty line, who would gain access to free full-day preschool with health, nutrition, and disability services built in. Their parents would gain a free, reliable full-day program in place of paid child care. Low-paid preschool and child care teachers would gain the bill's requirement that their salaries be comparable to kindergarten-through-12th-grade teachers [S4]. Head Start agencies and licensed child care providers would gain new funding streams and partnership grants [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and moderate-income families with young kids

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Education Secretary to give states matching grants, allotted by each state's share of four-year-olds from families at or below 200% of poverty, to run free prekindergarten programs for those children, with subgrants to school districts, Head Start programs, and licensed child care settings [S3].

Defines a qualifying program as full-day (at least 5 hours), with a maximum class of 20, no more than 10 children per instructional staff member, teachers holding bachelor's degrees, salaries comparable to K-12 teaching staff, and on-site health, nutrition, and family engagement services [S4].

Participation is voluntary for families, and states may use up to 15% of their grant for infant and toddler care and 20% in early years for quality improvements such as scholarships helping existing teachers earn bachelor's degrees [S4].

The bill amends the Head Start Act to fund Early Head Start partnerships with center-based and family child care providers serving children through age three, and gives those partnership grants priority in Early Head Start awards [S3].
States must run criminal background checks on all staff with direct access to children and bar employment of anyone convicted of a violent felony or violent or sexual crime against a minor [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through authorizations starting at $1.3 billion in fiscal 2015 and rising to $8.96 billion by fiscal 2019, and state governments, whose required matching share starts at 10% and climbs to 100% by the eighth year of the grant (with a reduced schedule for states that already serve at least half of eligible four-year-olds) [S4].

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes substantial new federal spending: $1.3 billion in fiscal 2015, growing to $8.96 billion in fiscal 2019 and 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2023, on top of growing state matching requirements that reach 100% of the federal grant by the eighth year [S4].

Every pre-K teacher would need a bachelor's degree, with current teachers having three years to comply; many experienced child care teachers without degrees could be pushed out of programs they already work in, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S4].

The bill creates new federally administered grant programs run jointly by the Education and Health and Human Services Secretaries, with state applications, performance measures, annual reporting, and federal approval of state plans, expanding federal oversight of an area traditionally run by states, families, and private providers [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and well-documented: quality full-day preschool for children from low-income families, plus free full-day care worth thousands of dollars a year to their parents. The main costs are money — a federal program growing toward $9 billion a year with state matches rising to dollar-for-dollar — and a credential rule that could displace many existing preschool teachers even as it raises pay for those who stay. The design is careful (voluntary participation, no punitive testing, diverse providers, background checks), but the cost and the federal-state structure were exactly the grounds on which the bill was never taken up.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and reported out of the Senate education committee the same day and placed on the Senate calendar, but with no cosponsors it was never brought up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced S. 2452 in the Senate on June 10, 2014 [S1].

That same day, the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which Harkin chaired, reported the bill to the Senate as an original measure without a written report, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 427 [S6].
No further action was ever taken; the bill sat on the Senate calendar until the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, without ever receiving a floor vote in either chamber [S6].

The bill authorized its prekindergarten grant program through fiscal 2023 and its development grants and Early Head Start partnership program through fiscal 2024, but no money was ever appropriated because the bill never became law [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, no one gained the preschool slots or the teacher pay raises it would have created. Federal and state budgets were spared the spending, and existing child care and preschool operators avoided the new bachelor's-degree and pay-parity requirements that would have come with the grants.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers spared the cost; providers avoided new rules

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.role: Chairman, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and, as committee chair, reported it to the Senate as an original measure the same day it was introduced, placing it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Made universal preschool a signature second-term proposal and pressed Congress to fund pre-K expansion, aligning the administration with this bill.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; it stayed on the calendar until the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate and House Republicans
against.role: Republican minorities in the Senate and majority in the House
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsorship or recorded support for the bill, and with Republicans holding the House majority it had no path to law even if the Senate had passed it.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken, so the split is inferred rather than recorded: the bill's only sponsor was a Democratic committee chair, it drew zero cosponsors from either party, and its fate was decided without a vote.

industries.industry: Private child care and preschool providers
industries.note: The bill opens a new public funding stream that licensed child care centers, family child care homes, and Head Start programs can tap through state subgrants and Early Head Start partnership grants, making them a permanent delivery channel for public pre-K. In exchange they would face Head Start-level performance standards, bachelor's-degree teacher requirements, criminal background checks, and K-12 pay parity — new revenue, but with compliance costs that could squeeze smaller providers [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Public school districts and K-12 teachers
industries.note: School districts are priority subgrantees and would gain funding to run pre-K programs, extending public education to four-year-olds. The pay-parity requirement would also raise preschool teachers' salaries to kindergarten-through-12th-grade levels [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Head Start and Early Head Start agencies
industries.note: The bill gives Early Head Start agencies new grant money to partner with child care providers and priority in Early Head Start awards, expanding their role in serving infants and toddlers through age three [S3].
